title: Rudin Ch 1: The Real and Complex Number Systems

items.back: A set with a relation $<$ such that for any $x,y$ exactly one of $x<y$, $x=y$, $y<x$ holds (trichotomy), and $x<y$, $y<z$ imply $x<z$.
$β$ is an upper bound of $E$ if $x ≤ β$ for every $x∈E$. $E$ is bounded above if it has one.
$α=\sup E$ means (i) $α$ is an upper bound of $E$, and (ii) if $γ<α$ then $γ$ is not an upper bound. The infimum is defined the same way with inequalities reversed.
Every nonempty subset that is bounded above has a supremum in the set. $ℚ$ fails this; $ℝ$ has it.
A field has $+$ and $·$ satisfying the usual axioms. An ordered field also satisfies: $y<z ⇒ x+y<x+z$, and $x>0, y>0 ⇒ xy>0$.
$R ∪ \{+∞, −∞\}$ with $−∞<x<+∞$. Every subset has a sup and inf here; $\sup ∅ = −∞$ by convention.
$z=a+bi$ with $i^{2}=−1$, $\bar z = a−bi$, $|z| = (z\bar z)^{1/2}$. $ℂ$ is a field but cannot be ordered.
Vectors $x=(x_{1},…,x_{k})$, inner product $x·y=Σ x_{i}y_{i}$, norm $|x|=(x·x)^{1/2}$.
No rational $p$ satisfies $p^{2}=2$. Worse, $\{p∈ℚ: p>0, p^{2}<2\}$ has no largest element and $\{p∈ℚ:p>0,p^{2}>2\}$ has no smallest.
items.classNote: Class proved $\sqrt2$ irrational with Euclid's lemma, and that $ℚ$ is not complete with a small-δ argument.
items.note: Motivates the whole book: $ℚ$ is an ordered field without the LUB property.

items.back: If $S$ has the least-upper-bound property and $B⊂S$ is nonempty and bounded below, then $\inf B$ exists and equals $\sup L$, where $L$ is the set of lower bounds of $B$.
items.classNote: Class proof: reflect the set, $\inf E = −\sup(−E)$.
items.note: You never need a separate “completeness for infima” axiom.
Exam proofs occasionally ask you to derive one of these from the axioms.

items.back: There is an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property containing $ℚ$ as a subfield. Rudin builds it from Dedekind cuts in the chapter appendix.
items.classNote: Stated only; the Dedekind-cut construction was not done.

items.back: If $x>0$ and $y∈ℝ$, there is a positive integer $n$ with $nx>y$.
items.note: The engine behind almost every “find $N$” argument.

items.back: If $x<y$ there is a rational $p$ with $x<p<y$.
For $x>0$ and integer $n>0$ there is exactly one positive real $y$ with $y^{n}=x$. Corollary: $(ab)^{1/n}=a^{1/n}b^{1/n}$.
$|z|≥0$ with equality iff $z=0$; $|zw|=|z||w|$; $|\mathrm{Re}\,z| ≤ |z|$; $|z+w| ≤ |z|+|w|$.

items.classNote: Real version in $ℝ^{k}$ only, proved with the quadratic $q(t)=|x−ty|^{2}$.
items.note: Gives $|x·y| ≤ |x||y|$ and then the triangle inequality in $ℝ^{k}$.
This makes $ℝ^{k}$ a metric space in Chapter 2.

items.back: $(A∪B)^{c}=A^{c}∩B^{c}$ and $(A∩B)^{c}=A^{c}∪B^{c}$. To prove $A=B$, prove $A⊂B$ and $B⊂A$.

Every nonempty subset of $ℕ$ has a least element (taken as an axiom). It implies induction: if $P(1)$ holds and $P(n)⇒P(n+1)$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n$. Example: $1+r+⋯+r^{n}=\dfrac{1−r^{n+1}}{1−r}$ for $r≠1$.
items.note: Also shown: a $2^{n}×2^{n}$ board missing one square can be tiled by L-trominoes.

items.back: A relation on $A×B$ is a subset $R⊂A×B$. An equivalence relation on $S$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; $[x]=\{y : y\,R\,x\}$ is the equivalence class of $x$.
items.note: Examples from class: “divides” is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; $<$ on $ℤ$ is transitive.

items.back: A fraction $m/n$ is the equivalence class of $(m,n)∈ℤ×(ℤ∖\{0\})$ under $(a,b)\sim(m,n)$ ⟺ $an=bm$. Addition and multiplication are well defined on classes, and $a/b$ is positive iff $ab>0$. With this, $ℚ$ is an ordered field.
items.note: Rudin takes $ℚ$ as given; this is extra.

items.back: $(a,b)<(p,q)$ iff $a<p$, or $a=p$ and $b<q$. It is an ordered set without the LUB property: $\{(0,a): a∈ℤ\}$ is bounded above by every $(1,b)$ but has no least upper bound.

items.front: Sups are unique; maxima are sups
items.back: A set has at most one supremum. If $E$ has a largest element, that element is $\sup E$.

items.front: $ℚ$ is not complete: the small-δ proof
items.back: If $x=\sup\{r∈ℚ: r>0, r^{2}<2\}$ were rational: $x^{2}=2$ is impossible; if $x^{2}<2$, then $x+δ$ with $δ=\tfrac12\min(x,\tfrac{2−x^{2}}{3x})$ is still in the set; if $x^{2}>2$, some $x−δ$ is a smaller upper bound.
If $a≤β$ for all $a∈A$ then $\sup A≤β$. But $a<β$ for all $a$ does not give $\sup A<β$. If $C⊂D$ then $\sup C≤\sup D$.
$\sup(A∪B)=\max\{\sup A,\sup B\}$ and $\sup(A+B)=\sup A+\sup B$ (worked in class with the ε-characterization).
Only $k=1,2$ carry a field product ($ℝ^{2}≅C$). $ℝ^{4}$ gives the quaternions, which are not commutative.

items.prompt: Prove: $ℚ$ has no largest element below $\sqrt2$.
items.modelProof: Given rational $p>0$, set $q = p − (p^{2}−2)/(p+2) = (2p+2)/(p+2)$. Then $q^{2}−2 = 2(p^{2}−2)/(p+2)^{2}$. So $q$ is rational, $q^{2}−2$ has the same sign as $p^{2}−2$, and $q>p$ exactly when $p^{2}<2$. Whatever $p$ you pick below $\sqrt2$, $q$ is a bigger rational still below it.

items.prompt: Prove: Archimedean property from the LUB property.
items.modelProof: Suppose $nx ≤ y$ for every $n$. Then $A=\{nx\}$ is bounded above, so $α=\sup A$ exists. Since $x>0$, $α−x<α$ is not an upper bound, so $α−x<mx$ for some $m$. Then $α<(m+1)x ∈ A$, contradicting that $α$ is an upper bound.

items.prompt: Prove: Density of $ℚ$.
items.modelProof: By Archimedes pick $n$ with $n(y−x)>1$, and integers $m_{1}, m_{2}$ with $−m_{2}<nx<m_{1}$. Then some integer $m$ satisfies $m−1 ≤ nx < m$. So $nx<m ≤ nx+1<ny$, and $p=m/n$ works.
items.classNote: Class picks the smallest integer $m$ with $m/n>x$ (well-ordering).

items.prompt: Prove: Cauchy–Schwarz.
items.modelProof: Let $A=Σ|a_{j}|^{2}$, $B=Σ|b_{j}|^{2}$, $C=Σa_{j}\bar b_{j}$. If $B=0$ it is trivial. Otherwise expand $0 ≤ Σ|Ba_{j}−Cb_{j}|^{2} = B(AB−|C|^{2})$ and divide by $B>0$.

items.prompt: Prove: Two-step sup proof (quiz pattern).
items.modelProof: To show $\sup E = s$: (1) prove $x ≤ s$ for all $x∈E$. (2) Take any $β<s$ and produce $x∈E$ with $x>β$, usually by solving an inequality for $n$ and invoking Archimedes. Equivalent ε-form: for every $ε>0$ find $x∈E$ with $x>s−ε$.

items.prompt: Let $E=\{(2n+1)/(n+3) : n∈ℕ\}$. Find $\sup E$ and $\inf E$ and prove both from the definitions.
items.modelProof: The terms increase in $n$. $\inf E = 3/4$, attained at $n=1$, and it is a lower bound since $5/(n+3) ≤ 5/4$. $\sup E = 2$: it is an upper bound since $5/(n+3)>0$. If $β<2$, choose $n>5/(2−β)−3$ (Archimedes); then $5/(n+3)<2−β$, so the term exceeds $β$.

items.prompt: Let $A$ be nonempty and bounded above and $c>0$. Prove $\sup(cA)=c\sup A$.
items.hint: Mirror quiz problem 4, but the inequality does not flip.
items.modelProof: $a ≤ \sup A$ gives $ca ≤ c\sup A$, an upper bound. If $β<c\sup A$ then $β/c<\sup A$, so some $a∈A$ has $a>β/c$, i.e. $ca>β$.

items.prompt: Prove there is no rational $r$ with $r^{3}=2$.
items.modelProof: $m^{3}=2n^{3}$ makes $m^{3}$ even, so $m$ is even, $m=2k$. Then $8k^{3}=2n^{3}$, so $n^{3}=4k^{3}$ is even and $n$ is even, contradicting lowest terms.

items.prompt: Prove that for $x,y∈ℝ^{k}$, $||x|−|y|| ≤ |x−y|$.
Let $A,B$ be nonempty sets of reals with $a ≤ b$ for every $a∈A, b∈B$. Prove $\sup A ≤ \inf B$.
items.hint: Each $b$ is an upper bound of $A$.
items.modelProof: Every $b∈B$ is an upper bound of $A$, so $\sup A ≤ b$. Thus $\sup A$ is a lower bound of $B$, so $\sup A ≤ \inf B$.

items.prompt: If $z∈C$ and $|z|=1$, show $1/z=\bar z$. Then show $|z+w|^{2}=|z|^{2}+2\,\mathrm{Re}(z\bar w)+|w|^{2}$.
items.modelProof: $z\bar z=1$, so $\bar z$ is the inverse. For the identity expand $(z+w)(\bar z+\bar w)$ and note $z\bar w + \bar z w = 2\mathrm{Re}(z\bar w)$.

items.prompt: From L1.1 (“check at home”): show $(a,b)\sim(m,n)$ ⟺ $an=bm$ is an equivalence relation on $ℤ×(ℤ∖\{0\})$.
items.hint: Transitivity is the only real step; you'll need $n≠0$.
items.modelProof: Reflexive: $ab=ba$. Symmetric: $an=bm ⇒ mb=na$. Transitive: if $an=bm$ and $mq=np$, then $anq=bmq=bnp$, so $n(aq−bp)=0$; since $n≠0$, $aq=bp$.

items.prompt: From L1.2: in $ℤ×ℤ$ with the lexicographic order, show $A=\{(0,a): a∈ℤ\}$ has upper bounds but no least upper bound.
items.hint: What can the first coordinate of an upper bound be?
items.modelProof: $(1,b)$ is an upper bound for any $b$. If $(x,y)$ is an upper bound then $x≥1$ (if $x≤0$, the element $(0,y+1)$ or $(0,0)$ beats it). But then $(x,y−1)$ is a smaller upper bound, so none is least.

items.prompt: From L2.1's warning: give a set $A$ with $a<1$ for every $a∈A$ but $\sup A=1$.
items.modelProof: $A=\{1−1/n\}$. Each element is below 1, and by Archimedes nothing smaller than 1 is an upper bound.

items.prompt: If $\sup A$ exists and $\sup A ∉ A$, then $A$ is infinite.
items.explanation: A finite nonempty set contains its maximum, which is its sup. So if the sup is missing from $A$, $A$ can't be finite.

items.prompt: For nonempty sets bounded above, $\sup(A+B)=\sup A+\sup B$, where $A+B=\{a+b\}$.
items.explanation: $a+b ≤ \sup A+\sup B$ gives one direction. For the other, given $ε$ pick $a>\sup A−ε/2$ and $b>\sup B−ε/2$.

items.prompt: $\sup(AB) = \sup A · \sup B$, where $AB=\{ab : a∈A,b∈B\}$.
items.explanation: Take $A=B=\{−1,0\}$. Then $\sup A · \sup B = 0$ but $AB=\{0,1\}$ has sup 1. The identity does hold when all elements are nonnegative.

items.prompt: If $x < y+ε$ for every $ε>0$, then $x<y$.
items.explanation: $x=y$ satisfies the hypothesis. The correct conclusion is $x ≤ y$ (compare B 2.1.9).

items.prompt: Between two distinct reals there are infinitely many rationals.
items.explanation: Apply density to get $p_{1}∈(x,y)$, then again in $(x,p_{1})$, and so on.

items.prompt: Every nonempty subset of $ℚ$ that is bounded above has a supremum in $ℝ$.
items.explanation: It is a subset of $ℝ$, and $ℝ$ has the LUB property. The sup just may not be rational.

items.prompt: If $x,y∈ℝ^{k}$ and $|x+y|=|x|+|y|$, then $x=y$.
items.explanation: $x=(1,0)$, $y=(2,0)$. Equality holds exactly when one vector is a nonnegative multiple of the other.

items.prompt: If $A⊂ℝ$ is nonempty and bounded, $\sup A−\inf A = \sup\{|a−b| : a,b∈A\}$.
items.explanation: $|a−b| ≤ \sup A − \inf A$ always. For the reverse, pick $a$ near $\sup A$ and $b$ near $\inf A$.

lines: Each term is below 1, so 1 is an upper bound.
Then $n/(n+1) = 1/(1+ε) > 1−ε$, so nothing below 1 is an upper bound.
items.explanation: $1/ε$ is usually not a natural number, so “let $n=1/ε$” picks no element of the set. Fix: $n/(n+1)>1−ε$ ⟺ $n>1/ε−1$, and the Archimedean property supplies such an $n$.

lines: Let $E⊂ℚ$ be nonempty and bounded above.
Since $ℝ$ has the LUB property, $α=\sup E$ exists in $ℝ$.
Every element of $E$ is rational and $ℚ$ is dense in $ℝ$, so $α$ is rational too.
items.explanation: Density says rationals are near every real, not that a sup of rationals is rational. $E=\{p∈ℚ: p^{2}<2\}$ has $\sup E=\sqrt2 ∉ Q$.

items.claim: Archimedean property: if $x>0$ then $nx>y$ for some $n$.
lines: This is impossible because $ℕ$ is not bounded above.
items.explanation: “$N$ is not bounded above in $ℝ$” is the Archimedean property itself. The argument is circular; the real proof uses the LUB property (see Proofs).

items.name: $\{p∈ℚ : p>0,\ p^{2}<2\}$
items.details: Bounded above in $ℚ$ with no supremum in $ℚ$. The standard witness that $ℚ$ lacks the LUB property.

items.name: $\{1/n : n∈ℕ\}$
items.details: $\sup = 1$ is attained; $\inf = 0$ is not. Shows a sup or inf need not belong to the set.

items.name: Trying to order $ℂ$
items.details: In an ordered field $x^{2}>0$ for $x≠0$, so $−1 = i^{2} > 0$, while also $1>0$ gives $0=1+(−1)>0$. Contradiction, so $ℂ$ has no field order.

items.name: $\sqrt2 · \sqrt2 = 2$
items.details: Irrationals are not closed under multiplication (or addition: $\sqrt2 + (−\sqrt2)=0$).
